title: Pin the name tags up once
allegory: A KV cache is a corkboard at a party: every guest pins up a name tag and a note exactly once, each newcomer pins their own and reads the board to decide who to listen to, and nobody ever re-introduces themselves.
map: each guest already at the party
the name tag they pin up
its key vector, stored per layer and head
the note pinned under the tag
the newcomer's question, checked against every tag
the new token's query, scored against all cached keys
under the causal mask, past keys and values depend only on past tokens, so reuse is exact

chapters.name: Endless introductions
chapters.note: run the whole prompt again ... for every word?

cap.1: To write one more word, the model re-reads the whole text from the start and redoes every sum it already did. The longer the text, the slower each word.
cap.2: A naive loop feeds 'My life motto:', gets 'Always', then feeds the whole prompt plus 'Always' again. Everything about 'My' is recomputed, identically, every step.
cap.3: Uncached decoding re-runs the full forward pass over the growing prefix for each new token: every earlier position's activations are recomputed although none of them can change.

cap.1: Picture a party where each guest pins a name tag and a note to a corkboard, once. A newcomer adds theirs, reads the board, and nobody re-introduces themselves.
cap.2: Attention needs two things from earlier positions: keys (what they offer to be matched on) and values (what they pass on). Cache both per layer, then feed only the new token.
cap.3: At each layer, position t reads K and V from positions ≤ t. Those depend only on their own residual streams, which are already final, so caching per layer and appending is exact.

chapters.name: One new row
chapters.title: one layer's cache: only the last row is new

cap.1: Each step adds one row to the board. Only the newcomer's tag and note are worked out; every row above is simply read back.
cap.2: Per layer, the cache holds keys and values for every position so far; ARENA suggests one tensor shaped (2, batch, seq_len, n_heads, d_head) per layer. Each step appends a position.
cap.3: Per new token, projections and MLPs run on 1 position instead of n, but attention still reads all n cached K and V: scores are [query_pos=1, key_pos=cached_len+1].

cap.1: The newcomer's question is new, but every tag and note it reads was already on the board. Nothing an earlier guest pinned can depend on a later one.
cap.2: Only the new token's q, k and v are computed fresh. Old keys and values came from old tokens only, thanks to the causal mask, so reusing them gives the same output.
cap.3: Causality makes k_i and v_i functions of tokens ≤ i only, so cached attention is mathematically the same computation. Verify: cached and uncached decoding give identical token ids.

chapters.name: The wrong seat
chapters.verdict: Offset positions by the cached length, then check the tokens match.

cap.1: The trap: the newcomer walks in alone, so they get told 'you are seat 0'. Wrong seat, so every answer after drifts, and nothing complains.
cap.2: Feed one token and PosEmbed adds W_pos[0] to a token at position 47. The first token matches, then output drifts. Index W_pos[cached_len : cached_len + n_new].
cap.3: Absolute positional embeddings must be offset by the cached length; the causal mask has the mirror bug, so build it for cached_len + n_new keys. Assert cached and uncached ids match.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Why MQA and GQA exist: the cache is the bottleneck
KV cache vs activation cache: know which you read

cap.1: Text that appears word by word leans on this trick. And two different things get called 'cache': one for speed, one for looking inside a model.
cap.2: Shazeer (2019) showed decoding is slowed by hauling K and V out of memory; multi-query attention shares one K and V across heads to shrink it. Grouped-query attention came later.
cap.3: When you hook or steer a model during generation, the KV cache keeps K and V computed before any edit you add later, and the activation cache is a separate object. Know which you read.

coda.title: How much work does the cache save?

curves.label: no cache: positions run at step x
with cache: positions run at step x

readouts.label: positions run in total, no cache
positions run in total, with cache
keys the last step must still read (cache or not)

caption.1: Slide the prompt and reply lengths. Without a cache the work per word keeps climbing; with one it drops to one word after the prompt. Watch the total saved.
caption.2: No cache: step k re-runs n0 + k − 1 positions. With a cache: the prompt once, then one position per step. But the last step still reads every cached key and value.
caption.3: Totals: m·n0 + m(m−1)/2 versus n0 + m − 1 positions through MLPs and projections. Attention still reads n0 + m − 1 keys per step; that memory traffic is what MQA shrinks.

where_else: Beam search: beams share a prefix, so they can share cached keys and values, as long as nobody edits the cache in place
Multi-query and grouped-query attention: designs that exist to shrink this cache
Memoisation anywhere: keep a result that can never change instead of recomputing it

hamming.what: Saving every layer's keys and values for past tokens, so each new token is the only one pushed through the model.
hamming.when: Whenever a model generates text one token at a time; you build it once in [1.1], then it is a flag in the library.
hamming.why: Under a causal mask past keys and values can never change, so recomputing them is pure waste, and at scale the saved cache itself becomes the bottleneck.

object.title: The cache shelf
object.subtitle: One shelf per layer, one column per token so far; turn the knobs to generate words and to share keys across heads.

knobs.label: key/value heads per layer (8 = one per head)

cap.1: After reading the three-word prompt, every layer's shelf holds a key and a value for each prompt word.
cap.2: The prompt pass fills the cache: for each layer, K and V at positions 0 to 2. The tallest column is the one just added.
cap.3: Cache after prefill: per layer, K and V for all prompt positions. Column height ∝ bytes per position per layer.

cap.1: Three words later, each shelf has three more columns. Nothing already on the shelf was ever worked out again.
cap.2: Each decode step appends one column to every layer. Old columns are read back, never recomputed.
cap.3: Decode appends one position per layer per step; earlier entries are immutable under causal masking.

cap.1: The shelf keeps growing with the text, and every new word must read all of it. That reading, not the arithmetic, is the slow part.
cap.2: Every step reads the whole cache from memory. Shazeer (2019) found this loading, not compute, is what limits decoding speed.
cap.3: Incremental decoding is memory-bandwidth bound: each step streams all cached K and V through the attention computation.

cap.1: Multi-query attention: all the heads share one tag and one note per word, so every column shrinks to a sliver.
cap.2: MQA keeps one K and one V per layer instead of one per head: the cache shrinks by roughly a factor of n_heads.
cap.3: One shared K/V head reduces cache size and bandwidth about n_heads-fold, at a minor quality cost per Shazeer (2019).

cap.1: Grouped-query attention: a few shared tags per word, a middle ground between one per head and one for all.
cap.2: GQA uses a handful of K/V heads, each shared by a group of query heads: a middle ground between full heads and MQA.
cap.3: GQA interpolates between multi-head (kv = n_heads) and multi-query (kv = 1), trading cache size against quality.

predict.q: With a KV cache, what does the new token still do at each layer?

options.t: Compute its own q, k, v and read every cached key and value
Recompute all earlier keys and values

predict.why: Caching removes recomputation, not reading. The new query is still scored against every cached key.

predict.q: Cached and uncached generation agree on the first token, then drift apart. First suspect?

options.t: Positions not offset by the cached length

predict.why: Fed alone, the new token sits at input index 0 and gets W_pos[0] unless you offset by the cached length.

predict.q: Why share one key and value across all heads (multi-query attention)?

options.t: Decoding is limited by loading K and V, so a smaller cache is faster

predict.why: Shazeer (2019) showed incremental decoding is memory-bandwidth bound; shrinking the cache speeds it up with minor quality loss.

object.where: Anything that memoises work it will need again: web caches, dynamic programming tables, build caches.
